title: Massively parallel characterization of RNA G-quadruplex stability and molecular recognition.
data_url: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE296171 (raw counts + pool FASTA); processed label table in the journal supplement gkag821_supplemental_files.zip; extra gels/fluorescence data at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.33132299

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed the journal supplement (stG4_STable_2_ProcessedData.xlsx: 6,000 rows x 50 columns, sheet 'All Sequences Processed'; second sheet 'Mutation deltaWT Scores' 1,889 rows x 16 columns) and the GEO files (GSE296171_stG4_raw_counts.txt.gz = 6,000 rows x 66 count columns, 775 KB; pool FASTA = 6,000 entries, 58 KB). Confirmed: sequences present as plain ACGU strings, 0 duplicate sequences, 0 missing values in all 13 score columns, 5 pools (stG4 3,213 / nsG4_Mut 1,833 / neg_ns 709 / neg_AAA 216 / pUG 29), 6 parent natural sequences (VEGFA, U2AF2, ARHGEF12, HNRNPA2B1, EWSR1, PABPN1). I recomputed the published stability score from the deposited read counts (log2 of guanine-pool frequency over 7-deaza-guanine-pool frequency, +1 pseudocount, mean of 3 replicates) and it matched the published column at Spearman = 1.000. I measured replicate-replicate Spearman (0.982 synthetic pool, 0.947 natural 90-mers, 0.47-0.89 per mutational parent), read depth (10.9% of sequences under 10 reads in the guanine+KCl library), the positive control (mean score +0.53 / -1.21 / -3.11 for minimum G-tract GG / GGG / GGGG; AAA negative controls +1.46), and ran baseline models (3-mer gradient-boosted tree: Spearman 0.977 within the synthetic pool on a random split; 0.347 transferring to the 709 natural 90-mers; -0.11 to +0.25 within each mutational parent).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The wet-lab protocol (in vitro transcription with guanine vs 7-deaza-guanine, reverse-transcriptase stop conditions, RNA Bind-n-Seq for G3BP1 and FMRP, pyridostatin treatment), the statement that no read cutoff was applied for most analyses, the -2 score cut-off used to call folded rG4s, and the CC BY-NC licence line. The fluorescence-polarization Kd measurements on figshare were not downloaded.

a1_downloadable.note: Open download, no login: GEO GSE296171 (775 KB counts, 58 KB FASTA) and the Oxford University Press supplement zip; I fetched and opened all of them.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Thirteen ready-made label columns in the supplied spreadsheet, e.g. 'RT Stop Score in KCl (G in KCl/7dG in KCl)'. Nothing has to be constructed; I read them straight out of the file.

a3_inputs_present.note: Column 'Shortened Sequences' holds the literal RNA sequence (characters A, C, G, U only, 11-90 nucleotides). No accession lookups needed; verified in the file.

a4_units_stated.note: Every score column header names the ratio it is (log2 fold change of read frequency, guanine over 7-deaza-guanine, per condition); methods state the log2 and the pseudocount. Length is in nucleotides.

a5_enough_rows.note: 6,000 labelled sequences counted in both the spreadsheet and the GEO count matrix; 3,213 in the main designed pool, 1,833 single-nucleotide mutants, 709 natural 90-mers.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~3.2 MB (2.4 MB spreadsheet + 0.8 MB count matrix)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Whole dataset loads into pandas in under a second; the baseline 5-fold cross-validation I ran took 7 seconds on CPU.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Paper says ~3,000 synthetic rG4s; designed pool is 3,213. Spreadsheet rows (6,000) = GEO count rows (6,000) = FASTA entries (6,000). No disagreement found.

a8_label_provenance.note: Label is a physical sequencing measurement, not a model output: I reproduced the published score exactly (Spearman 1.000) from the deposited raw read counts. Caveat I verified: the score correlates with read depth (Spearman 0.79) because strong quadruplexes drop out of the guanine library, so read counts must never be used as a feature.

B1.why: One spreadsheet, 6,000 rows x 50 columns; GEO counts join 1:1 on the sequence ID (verified, 6,000/6,000 matched).

B2.why: xlsx and gzipped tsv both parsed first try with pandas/openpyxl; no manual fixing needed.

B3.why: All 13 labels already normalised by authors to log2 read-frequency ratios from one assay; verified by recomputing one exactly.

B4.why: I measured 10.9% of sequences under 10 reads in the guanine+KCl library; strongest quadruplexes are floored by the pseudocount, so a depth policy is needed.

B5.why: 0 duplicate sequences among 6,000; checked directly in the file.

B6.why: Every score column header spells out its formula and condition; pool identifier column documents all five sub-libraries.

C1.why: Transfer question measured both ways: designed-library rules give Spearman 0.35 on natural 90-mers and ~0 within mutational series; informative either outcome.

C2.why: rG4detector, G4RNA screener, G4Boost, G4STAB exist and are mostly open, but none trained on quantitative RNA mutational stability; searched, not assumed.

C3.why: Unique-application plus novel-data angle: this 2026 dataset has not been modelled, and it has labels (ligand and protein binding) no model predicts.

C4.why: Current route is wet-lab: in vitro transcription, reverse-transcriptase stop sequencing, or circular dichroism/thermal melting per sequence.

C5.why: I computed concrete baselines myself (3-mer tree Spearman 0.977 in-pool, 0.347 transfer, 0.674 within natural set) and rG4detector is runnable.

D1.why: RNA-FM and RiNALMo are open-weight RNA language models matching plain RNA sequence input; both publicly distributed (searched).

D2.why: 6,000 sequences of at most 90 nucleotides: embeddings cache once on CPU, heads train in minutes; my tree baseline took 7 seconds.

D3.why: Backbone weights are openly distributed, but the paper and its data carry CC BY-NC (non-commercial), verified in the article licence line.

E1.why: Hold out whole parent natural sequences and whole pools; both columns ('Pool Identifier', parent name inside 'Sequence Number') seen in the file.

E2.why: 5 pools and 6 parent natural sequences, 216-3,213 rows each; marginal, since only 4 parents have adequate read depth.

E3.why: Global mean and per-pool mean computable; I ran them (global-mean R-squared 0, label standard deviation 1.91 in the designed pool).

E4.why: Three replicates deposited; I measured replicate Spearman 0.982 (designed), 0.947 (natural 90-mers), 0.81-0.89 (four usable parents).

E5.why: Measured in the file: longer minimum G-tract gives lower score (+0.53/-1.21/-3.11) and 216 AAA controls sit at +1.46.

E6.why: Label shuffling and feature ablation are trivial here; the whole cross-validation run takes seconds on CPU.

E7.why: rG4-seq transcriptome reverse-transcriptase stalling data (Kwok et al., Nature Methods 2016) and the G4RNA database are independent sources (found by search).

E8.why: rG4detector's published AUROC 0.75 on rG4-seq detection is reproducible with their open code; also the paper's own G-tract trend, which I already reproduced.

G1.why: Sequences and gene symbols present, but no UniProt/Ensembl/genomic coordinates in the table; joining needs sequence mapping.

G2.why: Named partners: rG4-seq transcriptome map (Kwok 2016) and the G4RNA database of experimentally tested rG4s.

G3.why: Join by sequence alignment or gene symbol; one natural 90-mer can hit several transcript isoforms, so a collapse rule is needed.

G4.why: Combined question neither answers alone: do designed-oligo folding rules explain which rG4s actually stall reverse transcriptase in whole human transcriptomes?

H1.why: 925 explicit negative-control sequences (216 AAA, 709 natural non-quadruplex sites) plus the full non-folding end of the score range.

H2.why: One lab, in vitro only, human-derived natural sequences, and only 6 parent sequences for the mutational arm.

H3.why: Honest claim writable in one sentence, including the read-dropout exclusion I measured (10.9% under 10 reads).

H4.why: The paper explicitly discusses guanine-library read dropout for strong quadruplexes and the -2 score cut-off; I confirmed the dropout in the counts.

I1.why: Dominguez and Mustoe labs (authors), the rG4 field (Kwok, Balasubramanian groups), and G4-ligand medicinal chemists.

I2.why: Result decides which natural rG4s and which mutations are worth testing in the lab, and which transcripts a pyridostatin-like ligand would stabilise.

I3.why: Ranking metric (within-sequence Spearman, precision in the top 20) matches the actual decision of picking a few mutants to test.

I4.why: Within the designed pool a 3-mer tree already hits the noise ceiling (0.977 vs 0.982), so ML only earns its place on natural-context transfer.

J1.why: Real grouped splits, a transfer experiment, a frozen RNA language model plus head, and a measured noise ceiling to compare against.

J2.why: Strong textbook positive control (G-tract length, loop length) that I already reproduced; nonsense would be obvious.

J3.why: Even the cleaned benchmark table plus the measured failure of design rules on natural context is a shareable result.

J4.why: Three-week budget: one week for embeddings and splits, one for modelling, one for external validation and write-up.

J5.why: Kill condition stated in success_criteria (two weeks, no held-out parent above Spearman 0.25) but not yet written into NOTES.md.

existing_models.name: rG4detector (convolutional neural network, Nucleic Acids Research 2022)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported AUROC 0.75 for detecting rG4-forming sites in transcriptome rG4-seq data, versus 0.65 for G4Hunter, 0.63 for G4NN and 0.73 for cGcC; figures taken from the paper's abstract found by search, not from rerunning it.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Their abstract frames linking rG4 predictions to in-cell behaviour (stress granule formation) as the open direction; I did not read their discussion in full.

existing_models.name: G4RNA screener (bundles G4NN neural network, G4Hunter and cGcC rules)
existing_models.score_and_split: G4NN scored AUROC 0.63 and cGcC 0.73 in rG4detector's benchmark on rG4-seq data; it is a motif-independent classifier, not a quantitative stability regressor.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved; only the web-server description was found.

existing_models.name: G4Boost (gradient-boosted trees, BMC Bioinformatics 2022)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported over 93% accuracy and F1 0.96 for folding state and R-squared 0.95 (RMSE 4.28) for folding energy on its own data, which is largely DNA and thermodynamically derived rather than measured RNA variant stability.

existing_models.name: G4STAB (multi-input deep network, Bioinformatics 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported R-squared about 0.8 predicting DNA G-quadruplex melting temperature from sequence, salt and pH, trained on 2,382 DNA sequences; DNA not RNA, so it cannot be applied directly here.

existing_models.name: AGAPE (machine-learning workflow for G-quadruplex ligand stabilisation)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported about 91% accuracy using small-molecule descriptors; it predicts from the compound side, not from the RNA sequence, so it answers a different question.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Affinity-versus-selectivity trade-off named as the standing challenge in the G4-ligand literature found by search.

backbone.name: RNA-FM (RNA language model, about 100 million parameters), with RiNALMo (650 million parameters) as the larger alternative
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU: 6,000 sequences of at most 90 nucleotides embed once and cache in roughly 1-2 hours; heads train in seconds
backbone.licence: Both backbones are openly distributed; the dataset itself is CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial), verified in the article's licence line

integration.partner_dataset: rG4-seq transcriptome-wide reverse-transcriptase stalling map of human HeLa RNA (Kwok et al., Nature Methods 2016; reported 3,845 stalling sites in potassium and 13,423 with pyridostatin), plus the G4RNA database of experimentally tested rG4 sequences
integration.join_key: RNA sequence match (and gene symbol for the 6 parent sequences and the 709 natural 90-mers, which are named after their source genes in the ID column)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do the folding rules measured on a designed oligonucleotide library predict which rG4s actually stall reverse transcriptase inside a full human transcriptome, or only inside short synthetic contexts?

controls.positive_control: Minimum G-tract length must order the predictions the way I measured it in the file (mean score +0.53 for GG, -1.21 for GGG, -3.11 for GGGG), and the 216 AAA negative-control oligos (mean +1.46) must be predicted as the least folded.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the stability labels within each pool and confirm collapse to the per-pool mean; ablate to sequence length alone; confirm read depth is never used as a feature (it correlates with the label at Spearman 0.79 by construction).
controls.external_validation: rG4-seq transcriptome reverse-transcriptase stalling data (Kwok et al., Nature Methods 2016) and the G4RNA database; plus the internal train-on-designed, test-on-natural split that I already measured (Spearman 0.347).

honest_claim_h3: For human RNA G-quadruplex sequences measured in vitro by one lab with reverse-transcriptase stop sequencing, the model ranks how single-nucleotide changes and flanking sequence alter folding strength, among sequences with enough sequencing reads to score reliably, which excludes the very strongest quadruplexes that drop out of the guanine library.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the RNA letter sequence to predict how strongly a four-stranded G-quadruplex folds, and how one mutation changes it.
plain_idea.train_on: 6,000 RNA sequences of 11-90 letters in a single spreadsheet, which I counted: 3,213 designed quadruplex variants, 1,833 single-letter mutants of 6 natural human sequences, 709 natural 90-letter control sequences and 216 unstructured controls.
plain_idea.predict: A folding-strength number: the log2 ratio of how often a sequence is sequenced from a normal-guanine RNA pool versus a pool built with 7-deaza-guanine, a guanine lookalike that cannot form quadruplexes. I reproduced this column exactly (Spearman 1.000) from the deposited read counts, so it traces back to a physical sequencing measurement.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Labs designing RNA-targeted drugs, and anyone choosing which mutation to test at the bench, need to know which natural quadruplexes fold and which mutations break them; I measured that rules learned from the designed library rank mutations within a natural sequence at about zero correlation, so the useful part of the problem is genuinely open.

more_or_better_data.why: No existing rG4 model was trained on quantitative single-nucleotide mutational data: rG4detector learned from transcriptome rG4-seq site calls, and G4STAB from 2,382 DNA melting temperatures. This dataset gives 1,833 measured single-letter mutants of 6 natural human rG4s plus 3,213 designed variants on one common log2 scale, which I counted in the file.

confidence_score.why: Three replicates plus read depth let me compute a per-sequence error bar (replicate Spearman 0.982 designed, 0.947 natural, 0.47-0.89 per mutational parent), which none of the named models reports; but rG4detector is an 11-model ensemble, so it does emit a spread, just not a calibrated one.

models_beatable.why: G4Hunter (2016 rule) and G4NN (2017 shallow network) scored AUROC 0.65 and 0.63 in rG4detector's benchmark and are clearly beatable; rG4detector (2022 CNN, AUROC 0.75, open code) is current and honest, but it predicts site formation, not mutational ranking, so a direct head-to-head is not apples-to-apples.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The obvious extra data (rG4-seq transcriptome stalling scores) comes from a different lab, a different assay format and cellular RNA rather than a designed pool, and the existing models were evaluated on their own split, so the 'same quantity, same way, same split' conditions all fail.

label_elsewhere.sources: G4RNA database of experimentally tested rG4 sequences (known resource, found by search); rG4-seq and rG4-seeker transcriptome stalling sites from Kwok et al. 2016 (search result reports 3,845 sites in potassium, 13,423 with pyridostatin); QUADRatlas rG4 atlas (found by search); G4STAB's 2,382 DNA G-quadruplex melting temperatures (Bioinformatics 2025, found by search), which measure the same physical property but for DNA.
label_elsewhere.join_key: RNA sequence (exact or aligned match) and gene symbol; genomic coordinates for the transcriptome sources
label_elsewhere.why: Thousands of other rG4s have a measured folding read-out elsewhere, so a model trained here can be checked on sequences this lab never touched, although the read-outs are binary site calls or DNA melting temperatures rather than the same log2 score.

risks: The 1,833 mutational variants differ from their parent by a single letter, so a random split puts near-identical sequences in both training and test and inflates the score.

The designed pool is a combinatorial grid of G-tract and loop choices, so a random split puts the same design in train and test; I measured a 3-mer tree reaching Spearman 0.977 that way, essentially the replicate noise ceiling of 0.982.
The label is a ratio of read counts and correlates with raw read depth at Spearman 0.79, so any count-derived feature would leak the answer.
Sequences with almost no reads (10.9% have under 10 in the guanine+KCl library) are pinned to a pseudocount floor, so a model can learn 'this is a floor case' without learning folding.
The ligand and protein-binding labels come from the same sequencing libraries, so using one as a feature for another imports shared counting noise.

Pooled correlation across parent sequences flatters the model: I measured a pooled Spearman of 0.347 on the mutational set that is almost entirely between-parent offsets, with within-parent values of -0.11 to +0.25.
leakage_plan.split: Leave-one-parent-out over the 6 natural sequences (parent name parsed from the 'Sequence Number' column, which I saw in the file) and train-on-designed / test-on-natural using the 'Pool Identifier' column (also seen in the file); inside the designed pool, group by G-tract architecture using the CountG1-CountG4 columns. Report within-group Spearman, never pooled.
checks: Shuffle labels within each pool and confirm performance collapses to the per-pool mean.
Compute edit distance from each test sequence to its nearest training sequence and confirm no single-letter neighbours cross the split.
Train on read depth alone to show how much of the label it explains, then confirm it is excluded from the real feature set.
Report within-parent Spearman alongside pooled Spearman every time, since the two differ by about 0.35 here.
leakage_plan.verdict: Manageable: the split columns are all present in the file, and the one real trap (pooled versus within-group correlation, and single-letter neighbours) is already identified and measured.

success_criteria.metric: Within-parent Spearman correlation on held-out natural sequences, plus precision among the top 20 predicted destabilising mutations, because the user picks a handful of mutants to test at the bench rather than reading off absolute values.
success_criteria.baselines: Measured by me on this file: 3-mer gradient-boosted tree trained on the designed pool transfers to the 709 natural 90-mers at Spearman 0.347 and to within-parent mutational ranking at -0.11 to +0.25; a model trained within the natural 90-mers reaches 0.674; the global-mean dummy is 0 by construction.
success_criteria.success: Within-parent Spearman at or above 0.5 on each of the 4 adequately sequenced parents under leave-one-parent-out, and at or above 0.80 on held-out natural 90-mers against the 0.674 k-mer baseline.
success_criteria.kill: If after two weeks no model beats within-parent Spearman 0.25 on any held-out parent and held-out natural 90-mers stay under 0.70, stop and write up the negative transfer result.

ambitious.why: NAR publishes rG4 prediction methods (rG4detector appeared there) and would take a model that closes the designed-to-natural gap and is confirmed against independent transcriptome rG4-seq data.

realistic.why: A benchmark plus a frozen RNA-language-model predictor, showing where k-mer design rules break on natural sequence context, is exactly the methods-and-evaluation paper Bioinformatics runs.

fallback.why: Even a clean negative result (designed-library rG4 rules do not transfer to natural context, with a measured noise ceiling) plus the tidied benchmark table is publishable there as a resource and evaluation note.

pitch.headline: 6,000 RNA sequences with replicate-backed quadruplex folding scores, plus a ligand response and four protein-binding read-outs, in one 2.4 MB spreadsheet.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Thirteen measured columns on one common log2 scale for the same 6,000 sequences, including 1,833 single-letter mutants of 6 natural human quadruplexes. Replicate Spearman 0.982 designed and 0.947 natural, zero duplicate sequences. All verified in the files.
pitch.the_win: Rank mutations inside a natural quadruplex at Spearman 0.5 or better, where a 3-mer gradient-boosted tree trained on the designed library scores between -0.11 and +0.25 (both numbers measured by me).
pitch.even_if_it_fails: We would have shown, against a measured noise ceiling of 0.81-0.89 per sequence family, that designed-library folding rules do not transfer to natural sequence context, which is the open question the paper itself raises about flanking sequence.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Dominguez and Mustoe labs who produced the data, and G-quadruplex ligand chemists deciding which transcripts a pyridostatin-like compound will actually stabilise.

ml_idea: Freeze an open RNA language model (RNA-FM, or RiNALMo if CPU time allows), cache embeddings for all 6,000 sequences once, and fit a light head to predict the measured folding score. Train on the 3,213 designed variants and test on natural context: the 709 natural 90-mers and leave-one-parent-out over the 6 mutagenised natural quadruplexes, reporting within-group Spearman against the k-mer baselines I measured (0.347 transfer, 0.674 within-natural, ceiling 0.947). Secondary heads on the same cached embeddings predict the pyridostatin response (the difference between ligand and no-ligand scores, replicate Spearman 0.57-0.83) and FMRP and G3BP1 binding, none of which any published model predicts from sequence. Drop sequences under a read-depth threshold and never feed read counts as features.

effort.compute_note: I timed the real thing: loading both files and running a 5-fold gradient-boosted-tree cross-validation on 3,213 sequences by 85 k-mer features took 7 seconds on this laptop CPU. The 1-2 hour RNA-FM embedding figure is an estimate (6,000 sequences of at most 90 letters), not timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Already done: count how many natural-context rows survive a read-depth filter and check replicate agreement per parent. Result: 4 of 6 parents are usable (replicate Spearman 0.81-0.89) while ARHGEF12 and VEGFA are destroyed by guanine-library dropout (85% and 73% of their variants under 10 reads), leaving roughly 1,150 usable mutants plus 709 natural 90-mers.

verdict_reason: Every Part A killer passes on the files, not the abstract: 6,000 sequences with 13 ready-made label columns, zero duplicates, zero missing values, and a label I reproduced exactly (Spearman 1.000) from the deposited read counts, so provenance is a physical measurement. The naive version of the project is dead and I proved it in 7 seconds: a 3-mer gradient-boosted tree on a random split reaches Spearman 0.977 against a replicate ceiling of 0.982, so nothing is to be gained inside the designed pool. The live project is the transfer question, which I also measured: those same rules fall to 0.347 on 709 natural 90-mers and to about zero within each mutagenised natural quadruplex, while within-natural training reaches 0.674 and the ceiling is 0.947. That is a large, honest gap with grouped splits available in-file, strong positive controls I already reproduced, an independent validation set (rG4-seq), and three label families (stability, pyridostatin response, protein binding) no published model predicts from sequence. Main caveats: only 6 parent sequences (4 with usable read depth), one lab, in vitro only, and CC BY-NC licensing.
